plain_text:
It's no secret. Gaining management support makes it a lot easier to implement
new programs and initiatives. But how do you get managers in your organization
to support waste prevention? Unfortunately, there is no magic formula or even a
clear step-by-step process. Each business, public agency, school, or organization
will be different, but securing management buy-in is the best way to establish
organizational support for new changes and practices.

plain_text:
To be convinced to act, management will need information about the costs
and benefits of paper use reduction.
semantic_text: To be convinced to act, management will need information about the costs and benefits of paper use reduction.

plain_text:
Information about the financial and environmental benefits of reducing paper use
will help you “sell the program.” Economic benefits include the potential for savings
through waste prevented and disposed, and better buying choices. Environmental
benefits include reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and savings
in natural resources, energy, and water because fewer materials are used and
transported.
semantic_text: Information about the financial and environmental benefits of reducing paper use will help you “sell the program.” Economic benefits include the potential for savings through waste prevented and disposed, and better buying choices. plain_text:
A waste evaluation will help you identify the paper waste your organization generates
and its path through your facility, from point of purchase to ultimate disposal.
semantic_text: A waste evaluation will help you identify the paper waste your organization generates and its path through your facility, from point of purchase to ultimate disposal.

plain_text:
The evaluation can be as simple as a visual survey of your trash, or it can be a more
detailed process of sorting, weighing, and measuring the volume of all the materials
in your waste stream. It can also be as easy as looking at paper purchasing records.
semantic_text: The evaluation can be as simple as a visual survey of your trash, or it can be a more detailed process of sorting, weighing, and measuring the volume of all the materials in your waste stream. It can also be as easy as looking at paper purchasing records.

plain_text: Walk through your facility and note how and where paper is generated:
semantic_text: Walk through your facility and note how and where paper is generated:

plain_text:
• What type of work is done in each area?

• What activities produce paper waste?

• What type of waste is produced?

• What waste can be prevented, reused, or recycled?
semantic_text:

• What type of waste is produced?

• What waste can be prevented, reused, or recycled?

plain_text:
The data you gather can be used to establish a baseline for comparison after the
program is in place. If a waste evaluation is done at least once a year, for example,
you can track program results and identify any changes in practices to guide future
reduction, reuse, and recycling efforts. The more detailed the information, the more
you will be able to do with it.

plain_text:
Be sure to consider the paper
that is being shredded or recycled,
and look for opportunities to
reduce the amount of paper
generated in the first place.

Preventing waste is not only
better for the environment than
recycling, it saves money too.

plain_text:
One major reason that many
organizations implement waste
prevention strategies is to realize
long-term savings of money, labor,
and time. Discovering what your
organization's paper purchasing and
disposal habits are—combined with
what you learned from evaluating
your paper waste—allows you to
target inefficient areas in your use
of paper.
